/guides/benefits-pip.question: Can you claim PIP for arthritis?
/guides/benefits-pip.answer: Yes, you can claim Personal Independence Payment (PIP) for arthritis if joint pain, stiffness, or fatigue limits your daily living or mobility. Eligibility depends entirely on how arthritis impairs functional activities—such as washing, dressing, cooking, and walking—not on diagnosis alone. Claims require medical evidence and completing the DWP PIP2 questionnaire.
keyTakeaways: PIP depends on how arthritis affects daily living and mobility, not on the diagnosis alone.
Daily living and mobility are scored separately: 8 to 11 points gives the standard rate and 12 or more the enhanced rate.
PIP is not means-tested and you can claim while working.
Return the PIP2 form within 1 month; challenge a decision with mandatory reconsideration within 1 month, then a tribunal appeal.
/guides/benefits-pip.bodyHtml:
Official sources: GOV.UK: Personal Independence Payment, GOV.UK: How to claim PIP, the DWP PIP assessment guide and the DWP benefit and pension rates 2026 to 2027. Benefit rules can change, so always check the official pages before you claim.

Before you apply: if you are still deciding whether arthritis may qualify, read Can you get PIP for arthritis? That page is about eligibility, including rates checked against GOV.UK. This page is the claim itself. Use the Printable PIP evidence diary to record daily living and mobility for two to four weeks before you fill in the form.

Arthritis can make ordinary tasks harder, slower or more painful: getting dressed, cooking a meal, washing, managing tablets or walking to the shops. Personal Independence Payment (PIP) exists to help with the extra costs that come with this. Many people with arthritis are eligible but never claim, or are turned down because their form did not show the real impact. This guide covers the whole process, from checking whether you qualify to challenging a decision, so you know what to expect at each stage.

What is PIP, and what is it not?

  • It is for extra living costs if you have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability and find everyday tasks or getting around difficult.
  • It is not means-tested. GOV.UK states that the amount you get is not affected by your income or savings.
  • You can claim while working. PIP is not an out-of-work benefit.
  • It is tax free and usually paid every 4 weeks.
  • It is based on how your condition affects you, not on your diagnosis.

PIP has two parts. You can get one or both:

  • a daily living part, if you need help with everyday tasks
  • a mobility part, if you need help getting around

How much is PIP in 2026/27?

PartStandard (lower) weekly rateEnhanced (higher) weekly rate
Daily living£76.70£114.60
Mobility£30.30£80.00

Source: GOV.UK PIP guide and the DWP rates publication for 2026 to 2027. Adult Disability Payment in Scotland is paid at the same rates for 2026/27, according to mygov.scot.

Who can claim PIP?

According to GOV.UK, you can get PIP if all of the following apply:

  • you are 16 or over
  • you have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability
  • you have difficulty doing certain everyday tasks or getting around
  • you expect the difficulties to last for at least 12 months from when they started

You usually also need to be under State Pension age to make a new claim. If you are over State Pension age, you usually claim Attendance Allowance instead, unless you got PIP or Adult Disability Payment in the last 12 months. There are also residence rules: you usually need to have lived in England, Scotland or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years and be living in England or Wales when you apply.

The difficulty must happen most of the time. GOV.UK explains this means you expect to have difficulty on more than half of the days over a 12-month period. For arthritis with flares, this is the most important rule to understand, and it is explained below.

England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland

Where you liveBenefitRun byKey differences
England and WalesPIPDepartment for Work and Pensions (DWP)The process described in this guide
ScotlandAdult Disability Payment (ADP)Social Security ScotlandSeparate application (online, phone or paper); its own process for consultations and challenging decisions. Same 2026/27 rates as PIP
Northern IrelandPIPDepartment for CommunitiesSeparate phone lines and processes; see nidirect

If you move between Scotland and England or Wales, GOV.UK says you must tell the relevant agency and make a new claim for the other benefit. For example, if you move from England or Wales to Scotland, your PIP stops 13 weeks after you move, so apply for ADP as soon as possible.

How does the PIP points system work?

PIP is assessed against 12 activities: 10 daily living activities and 2 mobility activities. Each activity has a list of statements (called descriptors) worth different points. The PIP regulations set the thresholds, and the DWP assessment guide confirms them: 8 points for the standard rate and 12 points for the enhanced rate of each part.

  • 8 to 11 points in the daily living activities = standard rate of the daily living part
  • 12 points or more in the daily living activities = enhanced rate
  • The same thresholds (8 and 12) apply separately to the mobility activities
Daily living activitiesMobility activities
Preparing food; eating and drinking; managing medicines or treatments; washing and bathing; using the toilet; dressing and undressing; communicating; reading; mixing with other people; making budgeting decisionsPlanning and following a journey; moving around

The "reliably" test

This is where many arthritis claims are won or lost. The DWP assessment guide says you should only be treated as able to do an activity if you can do it reliably, which means:

  • safely, in a way that is unlikely to cause harm to you or anyone else
  • to an acceptable standard
  • repeatedly, as often as is reasonably needed
  • in a reasonable time, which means no more than twice as long as someone without your condition would normally take

So if you can get dressed, but it takes you 40 minutes and leaves you exhausted and in pain, or you can walk 50 metres once but not again that day, you should explain that.

Flares and fluctuating arthritis

The regulations look at which descriptor applies on more than 50% of days over the relevant period. If different descriptors apply on different days and none reaches 50% on its own, but scoring descriptors together cover more than half the days, the descriptor that applies for the highest proportion of days is used. In practice, describe what a typical week and month look like: how many bad days, what you can and cannot do on them, and how long flares last. A diary is the best way to show this; use our Printable PIP evidence diary.

Painkillers, aids and timing

The assessment guide also says assessors should consider whether you can do an activity when you need to. If painkillers let you get washed and dressed soon after waking, you may not score; if you have to wait a couple of hours for them to work, a scoring descriptor may apply. Using aids such as a perching stool, long-handled sponge, grab rails or a walking stick can score points if you need them to complete an activity reliably.

How can arthritis affect each PIP activity?

PIP scores 12 activities. This table lists each one, as named in the DWP assessment guide, with examples of what people with arthritis often need to describe. Only include what is true for you.

The 12 PIP activities and how arthritis can affect them
PIP activityPartHow arthritis can affect it: what to describe
1. Preparing foodDaily livingGripping and lifting pans, chopping, opening jars and packets, standing at the cooker; needing a perching stool or relying on a microwave.
2. Taking nutrition (eating and drinking)Daily livingCutting up food or lifting a cup with painful, stiff hands; needing adapted cutlery.
3. Managing therapy or monitoring a health conditionDaily livingHelp with injections such as methotrexate or biologics, opening blister packs, applying creams or doing prescribed exercises.
4. Washing and bathingDaily livingGetting in and out of the bath or shower, reaching feet, back and hair; needing a shower seat, bath board or someone nearby.
5. Managing toilet needs or incontinenceDaily livingGetting on and off the toilet and wiping; needing a raised seat, frame or rails.
6. Dressing and undressingDaily livingButtons, zips, socks, shoes and bras; how long it takes, and whether you need aids or another person's help.
7. Communicating verballyDaily livingArthritis does not usually affect this directly. Mention it if another condition affects speaking, hearing or understanding.
8. Reading and understanding signs, symbols and wordsDaily livingArthritis does not usually affect this directly. Mention eye conditions linked to inflammatory arthritis, such as uveitis, if they affect reading.
9. Engaging with other people face to faceDaily livingScored for mental health or cognitive difficulties. Mention it if pain-related anxiety or depression means you need support to be with people.
10. Making budgeting decisionsDaily livingScored for cognitive or mental health difficulties, not physical ones. Mention it only if this applies to you.
11. Planning and following journeysMobilityScored for mental health, cognitive or sensory difficulties, such as overwhelming anxiety about going out. Physical walking problems belong under moving around.
12. Moving aroundMobilityHow far you can walk reliably and repeatedly, at what pace, with what aid, and how you feel afterwards. More than 200 metres scores 0; 50 to 200 metres scores 4; 20 to 50 metres scores 8 unaided or 10 with an aid; 20 metres or less scores 12.

How do I claim PIP for arthritis, step by step?

  1. 1. Check you can claim. You must be 16 or over, usually under State Pension age for a new claim, and have difficulty with everyday tasks or getting around that you expect to last at least 12 months from when it started. In Scotland, apply for Adult Disability Payment instead.
  2. 2. Call the PIP new claims line. In England and Wales, call the DWP PIP new claims line on 0800 917 2222 (Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 917 2222), Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm, or write to Freepost DWP PIP 1. Have your National Insurance number, bank details and your GP or health worker's details ready. In some areas you can apply fully online.
  3. 3. Fill in the PIP2 "How your disability affects you" form. DWP emails you a link if you applied by phone, or posts the form, usually within 2 weeks. Return it within 1 month, or contact the PIP enquiry line if you need more time. For each activity, say whether you can do it safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time, on typical and flare days.
  4. 4. Send supporting evidence. Include what you already have, such as prescription lists, care plans, clinic letters, physiotherapy or occupational therapy reports, and a symptom diary. Do not miss the form deadline while waiting for new evidence.
  5. 5. Go to the assessment if you are invited. If DWP needs more information, a health professional assesses you at a centre, at home, by phone or by video call. It usually takes about 1 hour, the audio is recorded and you can bring someone with you.
  6. 6. Read your decision letter. Daily living and mobility are scored separately: 8 to 11 points gives the standard rate and 12 or more the enhanced rate of that part. The letter gives your award, first payment date and when it will be reviewed. A first award lasts between 9 months and 10 years.
  7. 7. Ask for mandatory reconsideration if you disagree. Ask DWP to look at the decision again, usually within 1 month of the date on your decision letter. It is free. Explain which activities you think were scored wrongly and send any new evidence.
  8. 8. Appeal to a tribunal. If you still disagree, appeal to the Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within 1 month of the date of your mandatory reconsideration notice. It is free and independent of DWP.

You can ask for someone to join your call or to call on your behalf (you need to be with them). You may also be able to get a home visit from a DWP officer to help with your claim; ask when you call.

Filling in the form: practical tips

  • Answer every question that applies to you, even if it seems obvious.
  • Describe a typical week, including bad days and how often they happen. Avoid describing only your best or worst day.
  • For each task, say whether you can do it safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time, and what happens if you try.
  • Mention pain, stiffness, fatigue, dropping things and falls.
  • List aids and adaptations you use or need, and help you get from other people (or need, even if you do not get it).
  • Give real examples: "On 4 or 5 days a week I cannot do up buttons or a bra; my partner helps me. Getting dressed takes me about 30 minutes and I have to sit down to rest."

What evidence helps a PIP claim?

  • Clinic letters from rheumatology, orthopaedics or pain services that describe your condition, treatment and its effects
  • Reports from a physiotherapist or occupational therapist describing function, aids and limits
  • Your prescription list, including injections and side effects
  • A statement from a carer, family member or friend who sees how you manage
  • A symptom and activity diary covering at least a couple of weeks

You do not need to pay for new medical reports. Send what you have and explain the gaps in your own words.

What happens at the PIP assessment?

GOV.UK says you might be invited to an assessment with a health professional if more information is needed. It can take place at an assessment centre, at your home, over the phone or by video call, and usually takes about 1 hour. You can have someone with you, such as a friend or support worker. The audio is recorded; if you do not want it recorded, contact the assessment provider using the details in your invitation letter. They may ask you to do some simple movements. Only do what you can do safely and without causing more pain, and say if something would hurt or you could not repeat it.

The decision and reviews

You will get a letter saying whether you will get PIP, the date of your first payment and when your claim will be reviewed. GOV.UK says a first award is between 9 months and 10 years, depending on whether your needs are likely to change. You keep getting PIP while a review is being carried out. Tell the PIP enquiry line straight away if your needs change, you go into hospital or a care home, or you plan to go abroad for more than 4 weeks.

What can I do if I disagree with the PIP decision?

  1. Mandatory reconsideration. Ask DWP to look at the decision again, usually within one month of the date on your decision letter. It is free.
  2. Appeal to a tribunal. If you are still unhappy, appeal to the Social Security and Child Support Tribunal within one month of your mandatory reconsideration notice. It is free and independent of DWP.

Our step-by-step PIP appeal guide explains how to build a strong challenge. In Scotland, ADP decisions are challenged through Social Security Scotland; in Northern Ireland, through the Department for Communities and The Appeals Service.

What else can a PIP award help you get?

GOV.UK lists extra help linked to PIP. Depending on your award, this can include:

  • a Blue Badge (in England you automatically qualify if you score 8 points or more in the "moving around" activity)
  • a vehicle tax discount or exemption
  • the Motability Scheme, if you get the enhanced (higher) mobility rate
  • a Disabled Persons Railcard, if you get either part
  • Carer's Allowance for someone who cares for you at least 35 hours a week, if you get the daily living part
  • extra amounts (disability premiums) in some means-tested benefits, and possible Council Tax and bus travel help from your council

You can get PIP at the same time as all other benefits except Armed Forces Independence Payment.

Free, independent help

These organisations give free benefits advice or information. We are not connected to them:

  • Citizens Advice (England, Wales), Citizens Advice Scotland and Advice NI for form-filling and challenges
  • Turn2us for a free benefits calculator and grants search
  • Scope and Disability Rights UK for disability benefits information
  • Your council's welfare rights service, if it has one

If you are not sure whether to apply, Can you get PIP for arthritis? covers eligibility. Stay on this page for the application itself, and use the Printable PIP evidence diary while you fill in the form.

faqs.q: Can I get PIP for arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, if arthritis makes everyday tasks or getting around difficult on most days and you expect this to last at least 12 months from when it started. PIP is based on how your condition affects you, not the diagnosis itself. Check the current rules on GOV.UK.

faqs.q: What is the PIP new claims phone number?
faqs.a: In England and Wales, call the DWP PIP new claims line on 0800 917 2222 (Relay UK: 18001 then 0800 917 2222), Monday to Friday, 8am to 5pm. You can also start a claim by writing to Freepost DWP PIP 1. Checked on GOV.UK on 11 November 2026.

PIP2 is the "How your disability affects you" form. DWP sends it after you start your claim, as an online link or by post (usually within 2 weeks). You should return it within 1 month; contact the PIP enquiry line if you need more time.

faqs.q: How many points do I need for PIP?
faqs.a: Daily living and mobility are scored separately. In each part, 8 to 11 points gives the standard rate and 12 or more gives the enhanced rate, according to the DWP PIP assessment guide.

faqs.q: How much PIP could I get in 2026/27?
faqs.a: The daily living part is £76.70 a week (standard) or £114.60 (enhanced). The mobility part is £30.30 (standard) or £80 (enhanced). Check the linked GOV.UK sources for current figures.

faqs.q: Will I need a PIP assessment?
faqs.a: Not always. GOV.UK says you might be invited to an assessment if DWP needs more information. It can be at an assessment centre, at home, by phone or by video call, usually takes about 1 hour, and you can bring someone with you.

faqs.q: Can I work and claim PIP?
faqs.a: Yes. PIP is not means-tested and is not an out-of-work benefit, so you can claim whether or not you work. Your income and savings do not affect it.

faqs.q: How do I show that my arthritis flares?
faqs.a: Describe a typical week and month: how many bad days you have, what you cannot do on them and how long flares last. PIP looks at which descriptor applies on more than half of days, so a diary covering several weeks is very helpful.

faqs.q: How long do I have to challenge a PIP decision?
faqs.a: You usually need to ask for mandatory reconsideration within one month of the date on your decision letter, and appeal to the tribunal within one month of your mandatory reconsideration notice.

faqs.q: What if I live in Scotland?
faqs.a: Working-age adults in Scotland apply for Adult Disability Payment from Social Security Scotland instead of PIP. It has daily living and mobility parts at the same 2026/27 rates.
No. PIP (and Adult Disability Payment in Scotland) is not affected by your income or savings, and you can claim while working.

faqs.q: What can I get if I am over State Pension age?
faqs.a: You cannot make a new PIP claim, but you can claim Attendance Allowance (Pension Age Disability Payment in Scotland) if you need help with personal care. Also check Pension Credit, which can unlock other help.

faqs.q: Can I get a grant to adapt my home?
faqs.a: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, you can apply to your council for a Disabled Facilities Grant. Scotland does not have Disabled Facilities Grants but has its own support for adaptations through councils.

Prescriptions are free for everyone in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. In England, arthritis does not give you a medical exemption, but a prescription prepayment certificate can cut costs if you need regular medicines.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay VAT on mobility aids?
faqs.a: Not usually, if you are disabled or have a long-term illness and the product is designed or adapted for your personal use. You need to confirm this in writing to the supplier.

faqs.q: Will claiming one benefit affect another?
faqs.a: It can. For example, Carer's Allowance can affect the benefits of the person you care for. Use a benefits calculator or get free advice before you claim.

faqs.q: Where can I get free help with forms?
faqs.a: Citizens Advice, local welfare rights services, Turn2us, Scope and Disability Rights UK provide free information. You should not need to pay for help with benefit forms.
